newsitem.title: USA: SEC eyeing NY senator's warnings on pay-to-play.
newsitem.headline: SEC eyeing NY senator's warnings on pay-to-play.

text.p: The SEC is taking "under consideration" a state senator's allegations that bond underwriters gave as much as $1 million to New York State and local political committees last year and in the process successfully evaded the federal government's ban on pay-to-play, an agency spokesman said.

Securities and Exchange Commission spokesman Chris Ullman also said that a rule approved by the agency in late 1994 already bars underwriters from making indirect contributions designed to curry favor with politicians that influence bond firm selections on multi-million-dollar bond offerings.

New York State Sen. Franz Leichter, D-Manhattan, issued a report Wednesday that "shows that the State Republican Party raised nearly $1 million in campaign contributions in 1995 and 1996 from municipal bond firms that have won underwriting business in New York," according to a press statement.

In doing so, the firms "successfully got around" the Municipal Securities Rulemaking Board's rule G-37, which bars muni dealers that make contributions - whether direct or indirect - to issuer clients from doing business for two years with those governments.
The board is a non-federal agency established by the SEC whose rules must be approved by the commission.

"We have not formally responded to Leichter yet," SEC's Ullman said. "We have an ongoing regulatory review of regulations under our jurisdiction and any kind of input we get from someone such as Sen. Leichter we certainly take into consideration. It's under consideration now."
"The key is that anything that is strictly or directly prohibited by rule G-37 is always indirectly prohibited as well. That was an important (feature) of the measure," Ullman said.
"When Levitt was in the private sector, the conventional wisdom was that pay-to-play was the state of affairs," Ullman said.

"Upon arriving (at SEC), he encouraged MSRB to enact these regulations, and he has been very pleased with the progress. The evidence is anecdotal, but the culture of pay-to-play has mostly been put to rest," he said. "It has worked wonders," Ullman said, quoting Levitt.
